title: Compartmentalized Queueing and Evacuation Protocol PRD (sketch)
content:
Purpose

This doc sketches a design for a Compartmentalized Queueing and Evacuation Protocol (CQEP) for Redwood Dedicated. CQEP aims to let reserved capacity customers get predictable latency under normal load, absorb short bursts with bounded impact, and perform controlled evacuation (preemption/soft-evict) during severe contention while preserving safety for high-fidelity workloads.

Why this is needed (problem statement)

Observed failure modes today for Dedicated pools:
- Single noisy workloads can cause long tail latency for other customers on the same pool.
- Simple headroom or burst-credit schemes either over-provision (costly) or cause blunt eviction during spikes.
- Rapid capacity eviction leads to cascading fallbacks to hosted models, spiking downstream costs and degrading SLAs.
- Operators need a repeatable, debuggable protocol to move workloads off hardware for maintenance or thermals without user-visible outages.

High-level goals

1) Predictable SLO compliance for pinned routes under steady-state.
2) Bounded impact from short bursts — let low-priority bursts run insofar as they don’t violate high priority latency SLOs.
3) Graceful evacuation mechanics: staged, observable, reversible.
4) Minimal operator intervention: automated scoring & policies, with manual overrides for incidents.
5) Clear economics: expose burst billing, grace-credit consumption, and fallbacks in reporting.

Non-goals

- This is not a billing model spec; it includes hooks for metering but leaves pricing design to finance.
- Not intended to replace long-term capacity planning or reserved-size contracts.

Key concepts and unique terms used in this doc

- Compartment: a logical queue slice within a physical Dedicated pool. Each compartment has a fidelity class (gold/silver/bronze), an isolation level, and a local headroom budget.
- Evacuation lane: a ranked set of actions taken to reduce load in a compartment (throttle, queued pause, soft-evict, hard-evict).
- Grace credits: short-lived tokens granted to customers for occasional bursts. Credits amortize across windows and decay if unused.
- Compute bridge: an on-demand thin routing layer that can proxy requests to a compatible alternate model family (lower-cost or hosted) during fallbacks.
- Preemption score: runtime-calculated numeric ranking indicating how expensive it is to evict/shift a request (based on model size, in-progress KV usage, request age, and SLA weight).

Design overview

1) Compartmentalized queueing
- Each Dedicated instance exposes N compartments (default N=4) implemented in the runtime scheduler. Workloads (routes) are mapped to compartments by policy (product mapping UI / API).
- Compartments are orthogonal to tenant boundaries: a single tenant route can pin to a compartment to get fidelity guarantees.
- Scheduler enforces per-compartment concurrency targets and tracks a short-window arrival distribution to decide when to open/close temporary extra concurrency slots.

2) Local headroom & grace credits
- Each compartment has a small local headroom pool expressed in GPU-seconds (or slot-seconds). Headroom is replenished slowly (configurable cadence) and used to let short bursts execute without impacting core SLOs.
- Grace credits are visible in Console; they are consumed first before any eviction. Admins can grant emergency top-ups.

3) Evacuation lanes (ordered actions)
- Throttle: apply finer-grained QPS smoothing in-compartment (milliseconds) to reduce p99 tail for high-fidelity requests.
- Queue pause: temporarily hold new requests in the compartment queue for X seconds, allowing in-flight requests to complete.
- Compute bridge routing: divert select requests to a compatible alternate serving target (e.g., a quantized model variant or hosted endpoint) when scoring suggests lower regret. Marked responses include a header for observability.
- Soft-evict: politely evict long-running preemptable requests by returning a structured fallback hint (retry-after / alt-route).
- Hard-evict: forcefully terminate lower-priority workloads to free resources; used only as last resort and logged as SLO-impacting.

4) Preemption scoring and policy engine
- Runtime continuously computes a preemption score per in-flight request. Inputs: request type (generation vs embedding), model memory pressure, KV cache state, age, route SLA weight, and estimated rebuild cost.
- Policy engine uses scores and compartment thresholds to pick which lane actions to take. Policies are two-layer: default (system) policy and tenant overrides (bounds only).

5) Observability and tooling
- New metrics: compartment_headroom, grace_credit_balance, preemption_score_histogram, evacuation_actions_total (by lane), compute_bridged_requests, fallback_rate_by_route.
- Tracing: every evacuation decision emits a structured trace span cross-referenced with route id and computation graph.
- Console: per-route timeline showing grace credit burn, recent evacuations, and recommendation (increase reservation, tighten concurrency).

Operational workflow (examples)

Scenario A: 45s unexpected burst for a silver compartment route - Arrival spike consumes local headroom, grace credits drop to 0, preemption scores for concurrent bronze requests increase. Policy triggers throttling and a short queue pause for bronze, allowing silver SLOs to stay intact. Console shows credit burn and recommends a temporary top-up.

Scenario B: urgent evacuation for hardware maintenance - Operator sets maintenance window; affected compartments move to evacuation mode. System first uses queue pause + throttle, then attempts compute bridge routing for long-running inferences (low-cost quantized variant). Only if still constrained do we soft-evict preemptable jobs. Post-evacuation, metrics show reclaimed GPU-seconds and per-route fallback events.

Safety and correctness considerations

- Deterministic ordering: evacuation lanes must be applied in a deterministic order to avoid flip-flopping during borderline conditions.
- Bounded latency regression: policy must guarantee that gold compartments never see regression beyond configured p95/p99 guardrails.
- KV cache continuity: for workloads where KV warming is expensive, preemption scoring must penalize evicting such requests; compute bridge selection must prefer targets preserving cache semantics where possible.

Implementation sketch (runtime + control plane interactions)

- Control plane: UI/API for mapping routes to compartments, adjusting headroom allocations, and issuing manual top-ups/evacuations. Stores policy objects (simple key-value rows, policy id).
- Serving runtime: compartment tag on each request, scheduler integrates compartment counters and headroom ledger, preemption scoring hook in work-stealing loop. Evacuation actions surfaced through a pluggable action executor.
- Router: lightweight compute bridge router that can translate route-to-route compatibility (model signatures) and add observability headers.

Rollout plan and migration strategy

1) Canary (internal tenants): deploy CQEP in a single-region Dedicated cluster with a select set of trusted internal tenants. Observe safe behavior and false positives.
2) Beta customers: opt-in for a few customers who want burst flexibility, with feature-flag gating and extra logging.
3) General availability: expose compartments via Console API and default per-pool N=2 to start.

Success metrics

- Reduction in multi-tenant p99 tail latency incidents attributed to noisy neighbors by >= 40% in canary clusters.
- Fraction of bursts absorbed by grace credits (vs causing soft-evict) target >= 65% in beta.
- Time-to-evacuate under maintenance goal: 95% of lanes cleared within configured maintenance window.

Open questions / tradeoffs

- Granularity of compartments: how many make sense across different GPU types? More compartments increase complexity but let us express finer isolation.
- Pricing integration: should grace credit top-ups be billable in real-time? If so, billing signals must be low-latency.
- Compute bridge model compatibility: what subset of model families guarantee acceptable quality degradation? Need product + ML validation.

Risks

- Overly aggressive soft-evict heuristics could surface confusing behavior to customers. Mitigation: conservative defaults + telemetry for early detection.
- Complexity in scheduler interactions with existing autoscalers. Mitigation: implement CQEP as a gentle shim that primarily controls request admission, not allocation of GPUs.

Next steps (near-term action items)

- Product: finalize policy schema and console UX mockups (owner: Priya).
- Infra: prototype compartment counters and headroom ledger in runtime (owner: Luis).
- Applied ML: evaluate quality delta for compute bridge targets across 3 representative models (owner: Omar).
- Eng ops: assemble canary customer list and incident playbook (owner: Maya).

Appendix: quick policy example (human-readable)

- Gold compartment: headroom=1000 slot-seconds/day, grace_decay=24h, maintenance_preference=avoid-evict.
- Silver compartment: headroom=400 slot-seconds/day, grace_decay=6h, maintenance_preference=bridge-first.
- Bronze compartment: headroom=100 slot-seconds/day, grace_decay=1h, maintenance_preference=evict-early.

End of sketch.

Notes: this is intentionally a working draft focusing on operational safety and clear semantics. The following revisions should add policy DSL examples, simulated runbooks, and a small prototype metric dashboard exported to Console.
